title: A study of people's experiences of wearing partial  dentures over time
official: A longitudinal validation of the Partial Denture Experience Questionnaire (p-DEQ)
summary:
Background and study aims
Losing teeth can affect many parts of a person's life, including their ability to eat, speak, and feel confident. For some people, it can make everyday activities, such as chewing and swallowing more difficult, and may affect their diet and overall health. Tooth loss can also have emotional impacts, with some people losing confidence or a loss of self-esteem. In some cases, the psychological experience has even been compared to coping with a bereavement.
The impact of tooth loss is different for everyone. Factors such as age, socio-economic and cultural beliefs can influence how people experience tooth loss. In some communities, for example, tooth loss is considered a normal part of ageing and so fewer impacts are reported, whereas in other communities’ tooth loss can be seen as deeply problematic.
Removable dentures are an affordable way to replace missing teeth. Dentures can help people to chew food more easily, enhance appearance,  communicate more clearly, increase confidence and self-esteem. Being able to smile and without embarrassment has been linked with improved wellbeing. Successfully adapting to dentures can give patients a sense of achievement, and some come to see them as an "old friend," especially when the denture is fully incorporated into their everyday life. 
Sometimes, adjusting to dentures can be challenging. Some people may find that life with a denture is different from what they expected, and that it takes time to get used to wearing one. Common problems include discomfort, pain, food getting caught under the denture, and difficulties with cleaning and maintenance. Changes in taste can also have impacts on the enjoyment of food alongside problems with speech and being self-consciousness of the denture moving or slipping. 
There is, to date, no comprehensive patient-centred questionnaire specifically designed to fully capture the experiences of people who have lost teeth and who are living with removable partial dentures. It should measure not only practical issues, such as eating and speaking, but also the psychological, emotional and social impacts associated with living with a removable partial denture. 

Who can participate?
Patients aged 18 years and older attending for tooth extractions and provision of a new denture as well as those attending clinics for the provision of a replacement partial denture are eligible to take part in this study. 

What does the study involve?
The first phase of the study involves completing eight questionnaires at four timepoints (1, 4, 12  and 24 weeks after treatment). Participants who complete the first phase will be invited to take part in an interview.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Questionnaire participants will be able to see that we have developed tools to track progress in their care, they will see that we care about this and that we want to develop a rigorous approach to improvements in their care. They will be able to see that by taking part they are participating in these improvements. Completing questionnaires will also help them reflect on the progress they may be making in adapting to their denture. Interview participants may benefit from having time to sit and talk through the loss of their teeth and the replacement with a denture. They can talk through how their scores have changed, reflect on why this is the case and give us important information on what is a significant change. We will discuss how to shorten the questionnaire and make it more appropriate for use in routine dental clinics.

Where is the study run from?
The University of Sheffield (UK)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
October 2026 to February 2028

Who is funding the study?
Haleon Ltd (UK)

Who is the main contact?
Prof. Barry Gibson, b.j.gibson@sheffield.ac.uk

interventions.name:
This study utilises a concurrent mixed methods design, integrating a quantitative longitudinal validation study (WP1) with a nested qualitative study (WP2) exploring social and psychological adaptation to living with a denture in the UK and Ireland.
